uncited: Finite difference stencils compute the spatial gradient of a scalar volume by approximating partial derivatives using discrete samples from neighboring voxels.
This method solves the problem of estimating surface normals or density rates of change for ray marching and shading without requiring analytic derivatives of the underlying basis functions.

It differs from [Analytic Gradient Computation](2167-analytic-gradient-computation.md) by relying on numerical approximation rather than closed-form differentiation, and from [Gradient Estimation from Samples](2180-gradient-estimation-from-samples.md) by using fixed geometric offsets rather than statistical sampling of ray hits.
All finite difference stencils approximate the first derivative of a function $f(\mathbf{x})$ at a point $\mathbf{x}$ using a weighted sum of function values at discrete grid points.
where $w_k$ are weights and $\delta_k$ are offsets along the axis $\mathbf{e}_i$.
The accuracy of the stencil is determined by the order of the Taylor series expansion it matches.

Lower-order stencils (like forward/backward) use fewer samples but suffer from bias or lower accuracy, while higher-order stencils (like central or 4th-order) use more samples to reduce truncation error.
The choice of stencil dictates the number of memory accesses (samples) required per gradient component.
Central differences approximate the derivative using points on both sides of the target voxel.
In 3D, this requires 2 samples per axis (6 total for the full gradient vector).
It is second-order accurate ($O(h^2)$) and unbiased for interior points.
It is the standard choice for smooth volumes where boundary effects are minimal or handled separately.

It is first-order accurate ($O(h)$) and introduces a directional bias.

It is typically used when memory bandwidth is constrained or when computing gradients at boundaries where backward points are unavailable, though [Neumann Gradient](3342-neumann-gradient.md) offers a more robust boundary handling strategy.

Like forward differences, it is first-order accurate and biased.
It is the mirror counterpart to forward differences and is rarely used in isolation for volume rendering unless specific directional constraints exist.

Referenced in 'High Order Finite Difference and Finite Volume WENO Schemes and Discontinuous Galerkin Methods for CFD' (ICASE Report No 2001-11, page 6) and ICASE No 97-65 (Shu, 1997).
Finite difference methods are a cornerstone of numerical analysis, dating back to the early 20th century.
In the context of volume rendering, they were popularized as a practical alternative to analytic gradients for complex basis functions or sparse data structures like AMR (Adaptive Mesh Refinement).
